## Intent
Hypothesis: fusing integrate, decide, respawn, and render into a single register-only pass with no intermediate storage can approach the streaming ceiling by eliminating intermediate writes and keeping the death verdict hot.

## Layout & approach
The AoS layout offers 68 B/particle, of which the fused loop touches 48 B (70% hot — age, color, pos, seed, vel); the remaining 20 B is dead weight dragged through every cache line. No intermediate storage means the death verdict stays in registers, avoiding a second streaming pass — but the fusion bundles the byte-granular framebuffer scatter directly into the integration loop, mixing 68-B-stride particle streaming with random-byte writes to the framebuffer. The expected interaction with the cache hierarchy is that the particle working set spills L1d at N≈481, L2 at N≈7710, and L3 at N≈246723, but the framebuffer scatter is a separate, random-access stream whose footprint is independent of particle count.

## Cache saturation
The ns/particle is remarkably flat across all N: 22.98 ns/p at N=320 (L1d) vs 22.47 ns/p at N=10M (DRAM) at q=0.01. There is no spill knee. The L1d→L2 transition at N≈481 produces no visible cost increase (22.98→23.00). The L2→L3 transition at N≈7710 is equally invisible (24.40→24.26). Even the L3→DRAM transition at N≈246723 shows no rise (22.82→22.91). The dense grid resolves nothing because there is no cache-dependent behavior — the algo is frontend-bound, not memory-bound, so working-set size is irrelevant to cost.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth is 2.0–3.0 GB/s against a 12.69 GB/s ceiling — only 16–24% of ceiling. The memory floor is 5.359 ns/p, but the algo runs at 22.5–33.2 ns/p — 4.2–6.2x above the floor. This is overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound: frontend stall dominates at 63–67% across all regimes and death rates, with backend stall at 0%. Ratios vs baseline are 0.88–1.05x — essentially identical to naive scalar. At q=0.01, N=10M: 0.879x baseline. At q=0.5: 0.98–0.99x baseline. The winner (AF02.LP1-autovec) is 1.75–3.38x faster everywhere. Death rate is the primary cost driver: q=0.01→22.5 ns/p, q=0.5→33 ns/p — a 46% increase, because more particles trigger the respawn and render path with its byte-granular scatter.

## Assembly
The codegen is dominated by scalar operations: 293 insns/iter with 32 conditional branches. Only 15 vector instructions exist in the entire step function, and the loop digest shows mixed FP (vec 6 / scalar 20). The integration uses some vectorization (`vmovups`, `vmulps`, `vaddps`, `vshufps`, `vinsertps`) on the 68-B stride, but the render path is entirely scalar byte-granular: 28 `movzx` byte loads, 23 byte stores (`mov BYTE PTR`), each followed by `add`+`cmp`+`cmovae` for saturation clamping. The select-based respawn uses 12 `cmovae`. The `vucomiss`+`jae` chains for color clamping add 11 compare-and-branch sequences. This 293-insn footprint per 68-B particle starves the frontend, explaining the 65% frontend stall and the flat 2–3 GB/s regardless of cache level.

## Verdict
Refuted — the fused single-pass approach cannot approach the streaming ceiling. At 22.5–33.2 ns/p vs the 5.359 ns/p floor, the algo runs 4–6x above irreducible memory time. It matches naive scalar (0.88–1.05x baseline) and is 1.75–3.38x slower than the winner at every N×q point. The mechanism is frontend starvation: 293 insns/iter with 32 branches and byte-granular scatter produce 65% frontend stall, making the algo overhead-bound regardless of cache regime or death rate.
